rationale-baseline-frontmatter: regex shape risk depends on what the value carries, not the key. Unanchored frontmatter regexes for presence/enum keys (gate_policy, trajectory, workflow, rationale) are low-risk because the value space is bounded; for integer-valued keys they are high-risk because any \d+ substring in any quoted YAML value passes silently. When introducing a new value-bearing key into a file with existing pattern-match parsing, anchor your regex (^...m) even if the siblings aren't anchored — the precedent is wrong for this case. Confirmed by /falsify hypothesis 1 and shipped as 1.25.1 fix-in-scope.

rationale-baseline-frontmatter: falsification ritual value is highest immediately after authoring, not later. Phase 4 of this plan caught a real shipped-to-npm bug ten minutes after the publish that introduced it (1.25.0 → 1.25.1). The cheat-sheet effect is real (author has fresh memory of the code) but the cost of delaying is higher (cold context, lost intuition about seams). Run /falsify on the same session as the impl-complete moment whenever possible. Pattern complements eval-scorecard-format-fix retro's identification of the cheat-sheet effect — same-session ritual catches the bugs the next-day ritual would miss.

rationale-baseline-frontmatter: falsification fixtures must be MINIMAL — any validator rule that fires before the targeted one obscures the test signal. First version of the substring-attack fixture used workflow:feature without OTel/Context/Document gate sections; structural-completeness check fired before rationale-completeness, masking the actual hypothesis. Switched fixture to workflow:bugfix with only the gates that workflow demands. Rule of thumb: pick the workflow with the fewest required gates, include only the minimum sections, and ALWAYS assert stderr contains the specific rule name (not just exitCode) so you know which rule actually fired.

rationale-baseline-frontmatter: TS↔JS parity tests via subprocess are cheap and load-bearing. Pattern (shared fixtures → run TS validator + spawn JS hook → compare pass/fail decisions) worked first try, ~50 lines for production-grade parity coverage between apps/indusk-mcp/src/lib/trajectory/validator.ts and apps/indusk-mcp/hooks/validate-impl-structure.js. CLAUDE.md gotcha already named JS-port-mirrors-TS as a known risk; this plan operationalized parity coverage concretely. Reusable for any future TS-source-with-JS-port mirror in this codebase. The fact that fixtures are subprocess-spawned (not directly imported) means they exercise the actual hook execution path including frontmatter parsing.

rationale-baseline-frontmatter: would have anchored the regex on first authorship rather than waiting for /falsify to surface it. Mirrored the existing file's pattern (gate_policy:, rationale:, trajectory:, workflow: all use unanchored substring matches) without distinguishing that those are presence/enum checks where the value space bounds false-positive risk. The new key is integer-valued so any \d+ substring passes. Author should pre-emptively distinguish between presence-check parsing patterns and value-extraction parsing patterns when adding to a file with established but limited regex conventions.

admin-ui-hosting: quarantine damaged state instead of silently overwriting it. readRegistry originally returned emptyRegistry() on malformed projects.json; next addProject would cleanly overwrite the damaged file with a single-entry registry, destroying all prior entries with no recovery path. Generalizable beyond registries.

admin-ui-hosting: schedule a falsification dogfood pass BEFORE marking a plan completed. section-shape: falsification on a 13-row plan added 4 trajectory rows that were all real bugs, not noise — body content injection, concurrent register race, missing TTL filter in catchup, sanitizer accepting control chars. section-shape: append-only markdown files need TWO coordinated git/parser changes to branch-merge cleanly — `.gitattributes` `merge=union` driver AND the parser must split delimiter-bounded blocks on heading boundaries. Union without parser-split eats one section into next; parser-split without union conflicts on trailing horizontal rule. Document as canonical pattern for any future branch-mergeable markdown.

section-shape: workbench mode shifts concurrency primitive from git to filesystem locks. Original handoff-multi-agent ADR's "git mediates concurrency" was true for single-repo mode but quietly false for workbench mode (the .indusk/ dir lives outside the wrapped repo). The file lock is load-bearing in workbench mode, not redundant with merge=union. CLAUDE.md gotcha entry now documents this.

section-shape: "atomic rename" misleads when documented without distinguishing the two guarantees — it prevents torn-write reads (a reader never sees a half-written file) but does NOT serialize read-modify-write (a writer can still clobber another writer's not-yet-renamed result). Future docs for concurrency primitives should name the guarantees explicitly, not just the technique.

section-shape: would run falsification ritual on the parent handoff-multi-agent plan too (it shipped impl-complete pending falsification, never run). section-shape: would write Phase 0 trajectory tests as REAL failing tests against current code, not .skip() scaffolds. git-only-substrate: rip jj entirely, bring git to full semantic-graph parity. Two-phase: (A) delete defensive early-returns since sync engine dedup is already content-keyed via (path, blob_hash); (B) rip-out sweep across 14 getScm() call sites + jj.ts + jj.md + 5 skills + 25 prose refs. Driving motivation: dusk is scm:git and file-linkage edges are silently off, breaking files→episodes→entities traversal that Graphiti memory now depends on.

git-only-substrate: 13 assertions (5 Phase A parity + 8 Phase B rip-out) covering semantic-graph populates-on-git, graph_capture writes file-linkage edges, rebase→re-sync converges, rename detection preserves anchor UUIDs, plus rip-out checks (getScm/jj.ts/jj.md/skill dual-form/eval-trigger regex narrows/eval prompt git-only/indusk update nudges on scm:jj/docs supersede). Mechanisms: 4 e2e scripts share a tmp-project harness; 2 vitest integration; 6 source-grep; 1 CI. Zero deferred.

git-only-substrate: chose parity-via-deletion (drop 2 early-returns; content-keyed dedup handles rebase) + rip jj entirely. Rejected: keep-graceful-degrade (compounding debt), stable-event_id design (solves a problem the existing code doesn't have), jj-as-first-class (zero adoption). Targets 1.31.0 — structural shift, semver-major-feature for a "remove" change.

git-only-substrate: "graceful-degrade" is a design choice, not a hedge — re-examine it as the system evolves. The prior plan shipped option (c) graceful-degrade because "the semantic graph is not load-bearing." That framing rested on the 1.28.x agent loop. By 1.30, the agent loop had moved on, and the same "graceful-degrade" code was structurally broken. Defensive early-returns that don't fail loudly become dead documentation. The 5-minute spot-check that found "dedup is already content-keyed, the gap is two early-returns" should have happened during the prior plan's research, not during this one.

git-only-substrate: the Falsification ritual is the difference between "looks done" and "is done." T1-T13 all turned green; the 3 falsification hypotheses surfaced 3 real bugs (H1 missing init warning, H3 unhandled CLI stack trace on missing git, H5 pre-existing regex bug matching `git commit-tree`). Two were behavior the author created. One was inherited but not probed. Without falsification all three would have shipped silently. Plan authors write tests they can think of; falsification surfaces the gaps the author couldn't think of.

git-only-substrate: inherited bugs are still bugs you own. H5 (the `\bgit commit\b` regex matching `git commit-tree`) was pre-existing from the dual-form regex. Phase 2 narrowed it but didn't probe — and didn't notice JS's `\b` matches the `t`→`-` transition. Any refactor that touches a regex (or any input boundary) should include adversarial cases against the NEW shape, not just regression tests against the OLD shape.

git-only-substrate: probe the MCP wrapper layer during plan authoring, not Phase 1 execution. The 3 discovered early-returns in `tools/graph-tools.ts` and 2 in `bin/cli.ts` should have been in the original impl checklist. A `grep -rn "git mode\|getScm" apps/indusk-mcp/src/` during plan authoring would have caught all 5. Pattern: when a plan deletes a defensive check, grep for ALL instances of the check pattern across wrappers, not just the lib.

git-only-substrate: estimate-by-grep undercounted `getScm` call sites by ~30% because the symbol had comment + doc references the grep didn't surface. The research estimate was 14; the actual count was higher because tsc-strict caught references in system-tools, init, update, config doc comments. Future estimates should combine grep with a `tsc --noEmit` dry-run against a stub file that exports `undefined` for the symbol — that surfaces every consuming import, not just every keyword.

eval-agent-mcp-access: a fix that worked at the time can hide a second bug for 2 months. April's 3-highlights-processed verification was a fresh-spawn (the persistent session was new). Every commit since was a resume, which exercised a different prompt-construction path. The verification was correct for what it tested — but the test surface was 1 of 198 eval invocations. Future verification of background-process fixes should explicitly test BOTH first-run and subsequent-run code paths, especially when the runtime architecture distinguishes "first" from "subsequent" (catchup-vs-resume, fresh-vs-cached, cold-vs-warm).

eval-agent-mcp-access: per-commit success counters are cheaper than CI regressions for background processes. The brief's note that "CI for `claude --print` is impractical" was correct but didn't motivate a substitute. A single line-count check on `highlights-processed.jsonl` line growth would have surfaced the 2-month regression within days. Lesson: "CI is impractical → skip verification" is wrong. "CI is impractical → build a doctor" is right.

eval-agent-mcp-access: falsification rituals are particularly load-bearing for prompt-engineering work. Phase 5 found 3 hypotheses on top of Phase 4's source-grep test — all real bugs (backwards-anchoring phrasing, empty-list ambiguity, spawn-flag regression). Phase 7 found 1 hypothesis on top of Phase 6's happy-path test — also real (malformed-line bypass). Source-grep tests pin surface shape; falsification probes the boundary cases (phrasing, empty inputs, malformed inputs, persistent-session muscle memory). Without the rituals, the plan would have closed at Phase 4 with a known-incomplete fix.

eval-agent-mcp-access: prompt instructions are code with a softer compiler. Three of the four bugs in this plan were prompt-engineering bugs — the helper text didn't tell the agent precisely enough what to do in a specific scenario. Treat prompt instructions with the same rigor as code: probe phrasing, name edge cases explicitly, test that prompt behavior survives the agent's natural failure modes. Source-grep tests on prompt content are the equivalent of unit tests on code.

eval-agent-mcp-access: make T4-style runtime success counters a required exit criterion for plans whose verification path is "manual smoke against a live subprocess." Per-week or per-N-commits checks on success-side artifacts would have surfaced the 2-month regression within days of April's close. Concrete commitment for next similar plan: ship a `indusk eval doctor` subcommand as part of the fix, not as a follow-up.

eval-agent-mcp-access: inspect the eval session JSONL during Phase 1 diagnosis, not at Phase 6 in a panic. June's Phase 6 diagnosis went straight to the right answer (count tool calls in the session JSONL → 8 highlights_unprocessed calls vs 52 expected) within minutes. April's Phase 1 didn't look at the JSONL because the symptom seemed to be about tool availability not about agent behavior. The 7-line Python tool-call counter we used should be packaged as a permanent `indusk eval session-tools` subcommand — every eval-agent regression in the future starts with that question.

git-or-jj-substrate: PostToolUse hooks must check event.tool_response?.exit_code and skip when non-zero. Failed bash commands (failed git commits, rejected pre-commit hooks) still fire PostToolUse hooks, and downstream action against the previous-success state produces misleading scorecards / noise. Discovered in Phase 7 falsification as H4. The exit_code check belongs BEFORE the trigger-pattern check.

git-or-jj-substrate: compounding falsification rounds are roughly orthogonal — round N's findings aren't a subset of round N-1's. Phase 6 found H1+H2 (load-bearing brief claim wrong + UX gap). Phase 7 re-falsified Phase 6's fixes and found H3+H4+H5 (substring false-positive + missing exit_code check + init-before-SCM footgun) — three more real production-relevant bugs in code that had just been written and tested. Default for any plan touching infrastructure that fires on user actions: minimum two falsification rounds.

git-or-jj-substrate: MCP and CLI surfaces are independent SCM call sites and any SCM-aware behavior must be tested at both. Phase 6 H2-C discovered that mcp__indusk__graph_* tools went through apps/indusk-mcp/src/tools/graph-tools.ts directly, bypassing the CLI's getScm() branch. CLI fix didn't reach them. Pattern: any "fix the CLI to do X" must check whether MCP tools route through CLI or call the underlying functions directly.

git-or-jj-substrate: knowing what we know now, the dual-SCM model should have been skipped entirely. Had we picked git-only from the start, we'd have saved 6 weeks of dual-substrate maintenance + the eventual rip-out work in git-only-substrate. The dual-SCM choice was incomplete commitment ("don't want to break jj users yet") — but no jj users besides Sandy existed. The right framing at brief-time: "is jj a substrate we're committed to long-term, yes or no?" If no, drop it now. Don't ship dual.

git-or-jj-substrate: TDZ trap in persistent-evaluator.ts (Phase 3) — when adding new const declarations to a file with a withSpan(...) block, hoist any consts that span-callback code references ABOVE the try/withSpan block. Declaring after puts them in temporal dead zone when buildArgsAndPrompt runs inside the span callback. Cost: 5 evaluator-spans test failures before hoist landed. Generalizable to any "wrap action in observable span" pattern.

dawn-verify: `atdawn verify <plan> --phase N` — a detect-and-report-only phase-boundary verifier for work Dawn didn't execute (tier 3 of the enforcement ladder). Five detections: premature checkoff, skipped test-first duty, goalpost drift, red tests (row-level attribution via a new optional trajectory test-reference column), and phantom work (checkoff with no diff). Baseline comes from a chained verify ledger ({phase, sha, trajectory-hash}, merge-base bootstrap) rather than a pre-dispatch ceremony. Reverting/re-dispatch deliberately deferred to component 7. Research surfaced the sharper motivation: nothing in the system has EVER executed a test as part of gate enforcement — `passing` in the trajectory State column is an unverified self-report in every lane, including the two Dawn controls.

dawn-verify: 16 assertions + 1 explicitly-untestable (U1) covering `atdawn verify` — five detections (premature checkoff, skipped test-first duty, goalpost drift, red tests, phantom work), the clean path, a byte-identical-on-rejection guarantee (A7, the load-bearing invariant of the detect-only scope), a failure-safety ledger pair (A11 records nothing on rejection so a bad phase never becomes the next baseline; A12 refuses loudly on corruption because that failure would look exactly like success), unverifiable-row honesty (A13), backward compat (A14), non-git loud-fail (A15), and the keystone acceptance experiment (A16, manual, planted violation via an external agent). U1 — "boundary verification is sufficient for agents Dawn doesn't control" — is named untestable because it is a universal claim: A16 samples it once deliberately and the result is written into the Dawn master's component 6 row, with component 7 branching on it rather than assuming it.

dawn-verify: chose a read-only phase-boundary detector (`atdawn verify <plan> --phase N`) with a chained verify ledger for the baseline and runner-agnostic red-test detection — an optional trajectory `Test` column naming test FILES, executed via the project's own command, exit code as the verdict. Rejected the more precise test-title-tag approach (`it("[T7] …")` + JSON reporter parsing) specifically because it hardcodes runner knowledge into indusk-mcp core, against maxim 7 and the extensions-own-tool-knowledge convention; if file-level attribution proves too coarse it returns as an extension capability, not in core. Also rejected: detect+revert (couples the keystone to component 7 and to the revert semantics A11 already refuted), explicit pre-dispatch --snapshot (fails silently exactly when forgotten), baseline inference from git history, file:line references (brittle under refactor), and always-run-full-suite (maxim 4). Test execution scoped to referenced files by default with --full-suite opt-in; the accepted gap — no regression detection outside referenced files — is deliberately assigned to the Tier-2 judgment-checker horizon item rather than absorbed here.

This joins `agent-roles-phase4` (asserts a Key Decisions bullet the makeover compaction removed) and `daemon-identity` T22/T23 as known-red-on-main.

dawn-verify: dogfooding the finished tool on its own plan (`verify dawn-verify --phase 5`) produced 16 FALSE red-test findings while every referenced test passes. Root cause is two defects. (1) verify cannot distinguish "test file missing / not runnable" from "test ran and failed" — both are a non-zero exit and both report as red. That is the plan's OWN honesty principle applied inconsistently: it already reports an unreferenced row as `unverified` rather than `passing` (A13), but a reference that cannot be executed is equally a gap in evidence, not proof of failure. (2) `Test` path resolution is ambiguous in a monorepo — the command runs with cwd=repo root while the plan's own rows name package-relative paths, and nothing warns when a path resolves to nothing, so the author's most natural choice silently yields a wall of false reds. A16 compounds it by referencing matrix.md, a manual record with no executable form. Lesson shape: a detector that cannot tell "could not check" from "checked and failed" manufactures false confidence in the wrong direction — and the check that catches it is pointing the tool at itself, not more unit tests, because the fixtures all used repo-root-relative paths inside throwaway repos where the monorepo case never appears.

dawn-verify: a tool's own success artifact can silently disable the tool. `.indusk/verify/ledger.jsonl` is tracked and gets committed, so from the first clean verification onward it appears in every later phase's diff — which made phantom-work detection's "nothing but impl.md changed" test permanently false. Verify was switching itself off after its first success, and the symptom is indistinguishable from "everything is fine". Generalizes: any detection keyed on "what else changed since the baseline" must exclude its own bookkeeping from that comparison, the same way the commit cadence already excludes `.indusk/eval` from staging. Audit question for any stateful checker: does the artifact I write become an input to my own next decision?

dawn-verify: some invariants can only be protected structurally, not behaviorally. `resolveImplPath` was byte-equivalent in run.ts and verify.ts, and TERMINAL_STATES was defined in both probe.ts and detect.ts. Two identical copies pass every behavioral test right up until someone edits one — so a behavioral assertion cannot protect the invariant "these two lanes agree". The cleanup phase pinned them with tests that assert EXACTLY ONE DEFINITION EXISTS (a source-tree scan counting matches), which is the only shape that catches a divergence that has not happened yet. Use this when the rule is one that two enforcement paths must share: a copy there is not a duplicated line, it is a silent divergence waiting for the next edit.

dawn-verify: the ADR named the `Test` reference FORMAT but never its ANCHOR. It carefully litigated "files, not test names or line numbers" and rejected runner-output parsing on maxim-7 grounds — then never said what the paths are relative to. An under-specified decision reads as decided, so nobody revisits it: the gap survived the ADR review, the test plan, five phases, and 33 passing tests, and cost 16 false findings plus a convention the authoring plan itself violated. Hindsight rule: when an ADR settles a format, check that it also settles the format's frame of reference (base path, encoding, timezone, units). The half-specified decision is more dangerous than the open one because it does not look open.

dawn-verify: trajectory close audit — 26 rows, 0 blocked, 1 deferred (U1). lifecycle-rebalance: add a `Shape` check at the phase boundary in the Claude Code lane — local craft review (is this unit well-formed AS WRITTEN?) running after Verification, before Context, with findings appended as checklist items to the current phase. Ships as EXECUTOR BEHAVIOR, not a new gate type: no `#### Phase N Shape` heading, no validator rule, nothing retrofitted into 51 existing impls — precedent is `atdawn verify` (nobody writes "run verify" into a plan). Dodges a real hazard too: gate vocabulary is defined in 4 independent sites and an unrecognized `####` heading FAILS SILENTLY, misclassifying its items as implementation items. The load-bearing distinction that keeps Shape from colliding with Cleanup is operational, not taste: **Shape is intra-unit, Cleanup is inter-file**. dawn-verify supplies one example of each — the inline renderer was wrong at Phase 2 (Shape), while resolveImplPath duplicated across run and verify could not exist until Phase 2 built the second copy (Cleanup). Craft rules come from enabled domain extensions, not hardcoded. Sequenced FIRST (user's call) into the Claude Code lane so every subsequent plan, including Dawn's remaining components, is built with craft feedback already running.

lifecycle-rebalance: 11 assertions + 2 explicitly untestable, covering the Shape check. Structural decision forced by writing it: Shape ships as executor behavior and the executor is a SKILL (markdown, not code), so prose cannot be unit-tested — every deterministic decision goes into `lib/shape/` and the skill orchestrates, mirroring how /cleanup uses lib/cleanup/oversized.ts. A8+A9 are a deliberate pair pinning the intra-unit/inter-file boundary from opposite sides (Shape does NOT flag cross-file duplication; /cleanup still does) — without A9, "Shape ignores it" could mean nobody catches it. A4/A6/A7 are the anti-nag guards: well-shaped code must produce zero items AND say so; "nothing to do" and "reviewed and left alone" must be recorded, never silent — the dawn-verify rule that a check unable to distinguish "nothing to do" from "did not run" reports the shape of success without doing the work. U1 (does Shape flag what a thoughtful reviewer would?) has NO oracle and is carried with a concrete trigger instead: finding + false-positive counts recorded in each retrospective's Quality Ratchet, and two consecutive plans with human-judged-wrong findings reopens calibration as a falsification hypothesis.

lifecycle-rebalance: chose a per-phase `Shape` check performed BY THE EXECUTING AGENT ITSELF — rejected heuristics and rejected a spawned checker subagent. The decisive argument is that extension craft rules are PROSE ("minimize use-client boundaries", "one component per file"), and prose rules need a reader that understands prose; a heuristic engine cannot consume them, so heuristics would force re-expressing every rule as machine-readable config, duplicating knowledge and breaking the extensions-own-tool-knowledge convention (same maxim-7 argument that kept runner-output parsing out of atdawn verify). Heuristics also would have missed the motivating case outright — dawn-verify's inline renderer was ~15 lines, invisible to any length threshold. And the cost objection dissolves rather than trading off: in the Claude Code lane the executor IS already a model, so the review costs no extra call; a spawned checker would import the thin lane's cost model into a lane that doesn't have it, so that cost gets paid by the port plan instead. Also decided: executor behavior not a gate type (4 closed vocab sites, unknown headings fail SILENTLY by misclassifying items as implementation); findings append as checklist items (non-ignorable but non-blocking — a judgment false positive must not halt an unattended run); Shape intra-unit vs Cleanup inter-file, pinned from both sides by A8/A9; and a GENERIC phase-boundary record ({plan,phase,sha,at}) rather than a Shape-specific marker, so verify and Challenge read the same artifact instead of spawning a family of near-identical ledgers.

lifecycle-rebalance: 41 passing tests over a feature nobody could run — lib/shape absent from package.json exports, documented tsx command broken twice over (not on PATH, top-level await unsupported), never executed once. test-phase-structure: make test authoring a real phase — `### Test Phase N` alongside `### Build Phase N`, Test Phase 1 mandatory and first, additional test phases each justified in Test Phase 1. Motivated by measurement: 59% of 444 trajectory rows are Writable at Phase 0 and check-gates' `=== advancingPhase` can never match them, so the default path of the system's central discipline is entirely unenforced while only the 41% exception is guarded. Backward compat via an optional `Build ` prefix so all 52 existing impls parse unchanged.

test-phase-structure: 16 assertions + 2 declared untestable, covering test-phase structure, the justify-in-Test-Phase-1 rule, Gate A's Phase 0 blind spot, and both-lane parity. A4 is the stop condition (all 52 existing impls must validate unchanged, asserted over the real corpus not a fixture). U1's control was strengthened from an attestation to a durable artifact: Test Phase 1 cannot close until its deferred test bodies are reviewed, and the evidence is the code block in the impl rather than runner output that vanishes.

Plan lifecycle decision (2026-08-11): plans get a `monitor` state and become reopenable — build → release → monitor ⇄ reopen(maintenance phase) → close → archive, with a telemetry violation naming an expectation as the reopen trigger. Rejected midnight's `subsystem` primitive: closed stays the resting state so the active surface doesn't grow unbounded, which is what the makeover's decay layer exists to prevent. Subsystems get built only if an expectation appears that genuinely belongs to no plan — evidence, not prediction. `monitor` has no exit condition without telemetry, which is what makes it a real state rather than a waiting room; it was already in Dawn's Horizon as "the ninth loop stage."

test-phase-structure: chose two phase kinds (`### Test Phase N` / `### Build Phase N`, Test Phase 1 mandatory and first, deferrals justified there and optionally carrying the deferred test's body) — rejected overloading `Phase 0` (already used for prereq build work in 7 impls), rejected the `===`→`<=` operator patch alone (closes the enforcement hole, leaves the document illegible), rejected migrating 52 impls (optional `Build ` prefix makes it free), and rejected classifying runner output to detect fake reds (would put runner knowledge in core, the exact coupling `atdawn verify` refused). The load-bearing argument is inverted from the usual: consolidating the 7-copy phase-heading regex FIRST makes the honest structural fix cheaper than the patch that would have papered over it.

test-phase-structure: a test that asserts a REFUSAL catches a disabled rule; one that asserts acceptance cannot. Proven mid-plan — a reorder stranded the gate-completeness loop after the terminal process.exit(0), so it became dead code and returned exit 0 with no message, indistinguishable from "everything passed". Only the one case demanding a refusal went red. Corollaries: pin assertions to the rule's own message signature (a case passed because a DIFFERENT rule's message happened to quote an ID it looked for), and parity suites need paired accept/refuse fixtures or they pass against two implementations that refuse everything.

test-phase-structure: deliberate duplicates (a JS hook mirroring a TS module) diverge SILENTLY and in more than one way at once. Two copies of a trajectory parser drifted twice: one kept a local phase-reference regex so every row parsed as NaN and Gate A matched nothing; the other never produced a `state` field, invisible until the copies merged and every row read non-terminal. Neither failed loudly — a stale copy stops enforcing while everything downstream reports success. Pin such duplicates with a structural COUNT (assert exactly one definition), because no behavioural test catches a divergence that has not happened yet; and make the shared module's shape the UNION of what its callers need, since differing fields fail as silently as differing logic.

test-phase-structure: authoring the tests first found a contradiction the research/brief/ADR all missed — A1 ("an impl with no test phase is refused") and A4 ("every existing impl still validates") cannot both hold, because every existing impl has no test phase. Visible within minutes of executing the assertions; invisible across three design documents. The resolution (a `test_phases: required` frontmatter opt-in, mirroring `trajectory: required`) turned out to be the hinge the entire zero-migration story hung on.
